questions.statement: Which sentence places the auxiliary before the subject, as a yes/no question does?
questions.context: At the Colegio San Marcos in Heredia, a teacher checks what her class did for the school fair.

options.text: Did the students finish the poster for the fair?
options.feedback: Correct: the auxiliary did comes before the subject the students, which is the inverted question order.

options.text: The students finished the poster yesterday.
options.feedback: This is a statement, so the subject the students stays in front of the verb finished.

options.text: She has visited Cartago three times.
options.feedback: A statement with have as the main verb also keeps the subject first; no inversion is involved.

options.text: Never she has visited Cartago.
options.feedback: Placing the subject she right after never keeps statement order and misses the required inversion.

questions.explanation:
In yes/no questions the auxiliary verb comes before the subject: did the students finish it? Statements keep the subject first.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence correctly inverts after the negative adverb never?
questions.context: A coffee worker in Turrialba describes the harvest on her family farm.

options.text: Never she drinks coffee before dawn.
options.feedback: Keeping the subject she right after never leaves statement order, so this is not inversion.

options.text: Not only she works six days a week.
options.feedback: After not only the auxiliary should come first: not only does she work six days a week.

options.text: Never have I seen such a long harvest.
options.feedback: Correct: after a negative adverbial like never, the auxiliary have moves in front of the subject I.

options.text: Seldom the rain falls in Turrialba.
options.feedback: Seldom is negative, so the auxiliary must also be inverted here instead of following the adverbial.

questions.explanation:
After a negative or restrictive adverbial such as never, seldom or not only, the auxiliary moves in front of the subject.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which option forms a negative question with the auxiliary before the subject?
questions.context: A guide in Monteverde explains the cloud forest trails to visiting students.

options.text: Not you have visited the cloud forest before?
options.feedback: Leading with not and then the subject builds a statement pattern, not a negative question.

options.text: Haven't you visited the cloud forest before?
options.feedback: This is correct: the contracted auxiliary have not stands before the subject you.

options.text: Do you have visited the cloud forest before?
options.feedback: Do cannot support the present perfect, and negative questions put not after the subject, not before the verb.

options.text: You don't have visited the cloud forest before?
options.feedback: Here the auxiliary don't follows the subject, which is the order of a statement and not of a question.

questions.explanation:
Negative questions invert the auxiliary before the subject and place not after it: have you not finished the work?

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which of these questions has an inversion error?
questions.context: A high school student in Cartago asks her teacher about her English class.

options.text: Where does your brother study medicine?
options.feedback: This one is correct: the wh- word is followed by does, then the subject your brother.

options.text: Why did you choose English for that class?
options.feedback: This one is correct: did carries the past tense, so the base verb choose follows the subject you.

options.text: Which subject do you prefer most?
options.feedback: This one is correct: which + do + subject + verb is the standard pattern for a subject question.

options.text: What class your brother studies every morning?
options.feedback: The wh- word plus the subject leaves no place for the auxiliary, so the auxiliary is missing here.

questions.explanation:
Wh- questions invert auxiliary and subject: what class does he study? The question word and the subject never touch.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which question turns 'The books are due on Friday' into a yes/no question?
questions.context: A librarian in Alajuela reminds students about the return of borrowed books.

options.text: Are the books due on Friday?
options.feedback: Correct: are is moved in front of the subject the books, and the rest of the word order stays.

options.text: The books are due on Friday, yes?
options.feedback: Adding yes as a tag does not build a yes/no question and leaves the auxiliary after the subject.

options.text: Do the books due on Friday?
options.feedback: Do cannot stand before the adjective phrase due on Friday; this sentence needs a form of be.

options.text: Is due the books on Friday?
options.feedback: Swapping two words is not inversion: only the auxiliary itself moves to the front of the clause.

questions.explanation:
To make a yes/no question from a be-verb statement, move only the auxiliary in front of the subject and keep the rest.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which version drops if from 'If she had left earlier, she would have caught the bus'?
questions.context: A student in Liberia remembers the bus she missed during the rainy season.

options.text: If she had left earlier, she would have caught the bus.
options.feedback: The clause keeps if, so nothing is inverted and the two-clause conditional is still complete.

options.text: Had she left earlier, she would have caught the bus.
options.feedback: Correct: with if dropped, the past perfect auxiliary had is placed before the subject she.

options.text: Did she leave earlier, she would have caught the bus.
options.feedback: Did marks simple past, but this unreal situation needs the past perfect had plus the past participle left.

options.text: Would have she left earlier, she would have caught the bus.
options.feedback: Would have is the auxiliary of the result clause, so it cannot open the inverted conditional clause.

questions.explanation:
Drop if in a conditional and invert: the if-clause auxiliary (had, were, should) moves in front of the subject to mark unreal time.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence puts 'Only after the siren sounds' first, with inversion?
questions.context: A supervisor at a coffee processing plant in Naranjo watches the morning shift.

options.text: Only after the siren sounds the workers stop for lunch.
options.feedback: A fronted only after phrase needs the auxiliary do in front of the subject, not plain statement order.

options.text: Only after the siren sounds, stop the workers for lunch.
options.feedback: This has no subject at all, so it reads as a command; the real subject must follow the auxiliary do.

options.text: The workers only after the siren sounds stop for lunch.
options.feedback: Placing the subject before the fronted phrase breaks the pattern, because the auxiliary has to come first here.

options.text: Only after the siren sounds do the workers stop for lunch.
options.feedback: Correct: the fronted only after phrase triggers inversion, so do comes before the subject the workers.

questions.explanation:
When a restrictive or negative adverbial (only, never, not until, seldom) opens the clause, the auxiliary is inverted with it.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence gives the emphasis an editor wants with the phrase 'Not only'?
questions.context: An editor at a school newspaper in Heredia tightens a headline before printing it.

options.text: Not only did she win the national writing contest.
options.feedback: Correct: not only is fronted, so its auxiliary did moves in front of the subject she and stresses the second part.

options.text: Not only she did win the national writing contest.
options.feedback: Here not only stays in front of the full verb did win, which keeps statement order and kills the contrast.

options.text: She not only did win the national writing contest.
options.feedback: With the subject first the adverbial is not fronted, so the reader gets an ordinary statement with no contrast.

options.text: Not only won she the national writing contest.
options.feedback: Fronting not only cannot split the verb phrase won from its subject; only the auxiliary may move forward.

questions.explanation:
Fronting not only, never, seldom or only demands auxiliary inversion and puts the focus on the second element of the clause.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence stresses the time limit, with 'only after dark' fronted?
questions.context: A guide in Tortuguero explains when the night tour starts in the national park.

options.text: The tour starts only after dark.
options.feedback: The sentence is grammatically fine, but a mid-position only after gives no contrast or stress at all.

options.text: Only after dark the tour starts at the pier.
options.feedback: A fronted only after phrase requires the auxiliary before the subject, so statement order is not accepted.

options.text: Only after dark does the tour start at the pier.
options.feedback: Correct: only after dark is fronted, so the auxiliary does stands before the subject the tour.

options.text: Only after dark does start the tour at the pier.
options.feedback: Here does comes before the main verb start, which leaves the subject the tour with no place in the pattern.

questions.explanation:
A fronted only + time phrase is restrictive: it forces inversion (does, did) and it focuses attention on that limit.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which email sentence correctly repairs the draft 'Why you were absent'?
questions.context: A student in San Jose emails her English teacher about a class she missed.

options.text: Why you were absent last Monday?
options.feedback: The question word cannot be followed directly by the subject; the auxiliary were belongs in that slot.

options.text: Why were you absent last Monday?
options.feedback: This one is correct: why + were + you follows the inverted pattern for a wh- question whose subject is you.

options.text: Why did you absent last Monday?
options.feedback: Did cannot follow a form of be; since the sentence uses was, the main verb has to be the base form absent.

options.text: Why you did absent last Monday?
options.feedback: Placing the subject you right after why cancels the inversion and leaves the auxiliary without a place.

questions.explanation:
Wh- questions invert auxiliary and subject: why were you absent? The question word and the subject are never adjacent.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which opening expresses the unreal condition 'If I were in your place'?
questions.context: A student at the Teatro Nacional rehearses a speech for a school competition.

options.text: If I would be in your place, I would take the stage.
options.feedback: A fully unreal if-clause takes the subjunctive were, and would belongs only to the result clause.

options.text: Was I in your place, I would take the stage.
options.feedback: Was cannot open an unreal conditional clause; the inverted form must use were, the subjunctive of be.

options.text: Were I in your place, I would take the stage.
options.feedback: Correct: dropping if inverts the subjunctive were to the front, with the subject I right after it.

options.text: I were in your place, I would take the stage.
options.feedback: Removing if requires the auxiliary to move forward, so the subject I cannot stay in front of were.

questions.explanation:
Unreal conditions may drop if and invert were, had or should before the subject; this is formal but standard in writing.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence keeps formal inversion after the adverb rarely?
questions.context: A newspaper editor in San Jose chooses formal wording for an article about recycling.

options.text: Rarely does the council hold meetings on Fridays.
options.feedback: Correct: rarely is negative, so the auxiliary does is placed in front of the subject the council.

options.text: Rarely the council holds meetings on Fridays.
options.feedback: Here the subject follows the adverbial without any inversion, so the clause is only a statement.

options.text: Rarely the council does hold meetings on Fridays.
options.feedback: The full verb does hold stays after the subject; inversion moves only the auxiliary does to the front.

options.text: Rarely has the council meetings on Fridays.
options.feedback: Has cannot invert here because the main verb is the full verb holds, which needs the auxiliary does.

questions.explanation:
Negative adverbs such as rarely and seldom need subject-auxiliary inversion; only the auxiliary moves, the verb stays put.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which version inverts the if-clause of 'If you need a taxi, call the desk'?
questions.context: A hotel receptionist in Manuel Antonio offers extra services to a guest.

options.text: If you need a taxi, call the desk.
options.feedback: The if-clause is unchanged, so this is a normal conditional and shows no inverted structure at all.

options.text: You need a taxi, call the desk.
options.feedback: Removing if without inverting the auxiliary leaves the subject you in front, which is not allowed.

options.text: Need you a taxi, call the desk.
options.feedback: Only an auxiliary (should, could, would) can move before the subject; the main verb need cannot invert.

options.text: Should you need a taxi, call the desk.
options.feedback: Correct: should is the modal auxiliary of the if-clause, placed before the subject you for a polite offer.

questions.explanation:
Modal if-clauses can drop if and invert the modal: should you need it, tell me. The tone stays polite and formal.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence says that no ride happened at all, not simply that rides were rare?
questions.context: A cyclist in Guanacaste describes her early morning ride before sunrise.

options.text: Rarely she has ridden before sunrise.
options.feedback: Rarely means not often, and the subject she also stays before the auxiliary, so two features fail here.

options.text: Not once has she ridden before sunrise.
options.feedback: Correct: not once is a negative adverbial, so the auxiliary has is inverted before the subject she.

options.text: Not once she has ridden before sunrise.
options.feedback: Placing the subject she before the auxiliary has cancels the inversion that not once requires.

options.text: Seldom has she ridden before sunrise.
options.feedback: Seldom does express rarity, but it means not often, not the absolute zero that not once expresses.

questions.explanation:
Negative phrases differ in strength: never and not once mean zero occurrences, while rarely and seldom only reduce the frequency.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Her draft: 'Not until the rain stopped the buses moved again.' Which fix is right?
questions.context: A student from Alajuela submits a draft sentence to her teacher for correction.

options.text: Not until the rain stopped did move the buses again.
options.feedback: The subject the buses cannot follow the main verb move; after did it has to come before the verb.

options.text: Until the rain stopped, the buses not moved again.
options.feedback: Without a fronted negative phrase, normal word order applies, so not cannot sit in front of the main verb.

options.text: Not until the rain stopped did the buses move again.
options.feedback: Correct: not until opens the clause, so the auxiliary did is placed before the subject the buses.

options.text: Not until the rain stopped did the buses moved again.
options.feedback: Did already carries the past tense, so the main verb must be the base form move, not the participle moved.

questions.explanation:
A fronted not until phrase requires auxiliary inversion: did + subject + base verb. Did is never followed by a participle.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which yes/no question inverts 'There are still sandwiches in the fridge'?
questions.context: A cafeteria worker at a school in Escazu checks the leftovers at closing time.

options.text: Sandwiches are still there in the fridge?
options.feedback: This keeps the real subject sandwiches first, so the clause is a statement rather than an inverted question.

options.text: Are still sandwiches there in the fridge?
options.feedback: Here the real subject sandwiches sits right after the auxiliary, but there is the grammatical subject.

options.text: There are still sandwiches in the fridge?
options.feedback: Word order without inversion is not a question; the auxiliary must stand before the subject and the verb there.

options.text: Are there still sandwiches in the fridge?
options.feedback: Correct: in the there-construction there is the subject, so the auxiliary are is placed before it.

questions.explanation:
In there-constructions there is the grammatical subject, so the auxiliary inverts in front of it: are there sandwiches?

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which option does not use subject-auxiliary inversion with a fronted phrase?
questions.context: A journalist in San Jose writes a feature about extreme sports in La Paz.

options.text: No matter how much did he train, he never qualified.
options.feedback: No matter how is a concessive connector, so the clause needs statement order and inverting did here is wrong.

options.text: No matter how much he trained, he never qualified.
options.feedback: This one is correct: no matter how takes a full clause with the subject he before the verb trained.

options.text: No matter how many times did she jump, she fell.
options.feedback: This is wrong: after no matter how the auxiliary did and the subject she are inverted with no reason.

options.text: No matter how far walked they, they never rested.
options.feedback: Here the verb phrase is split, because only the auxiliary, never a verb, may stand before the subject.

questions.explanation:
Only negative or restrictive adverbials (never, rarely, not only, only then) force inversion; connectors like no matter how never do.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which headline correctly inverts after both rarely and not only?
questions.context: An editor at a Heredia news site checks a headline written under deadline.

options.text: Rarely does the mayor speak publicly; not only she ignores reporters.
options.feedback: The first clause inverts correctly, but after not only the auxiliary must also come before the subject she.

options.text: Rarely the mayor speaks publicly; not only does she ignore reporters.
options.feedback: After rarely the subject cannot follow the adverbial directly; the auxiliary does has to be inverted with it.

options.text: Rarely does the mayor speak publicly; not only does she ignore reporters.
options.feedback: Correct: both fronted negatives invert independently, so each clause carries its own auxiliary before the subject.

options.text: Rarely the mayor does speak publicly; not only does she ignores reporters.
options.feedback: Here rarely is not inverted, and not only is followed by a bare verb ignores, which no pattern allows.

questions.explanation:
Each fronted negative adverbial is independent: when a sentence has two of them, each clause needs its own auxiliary inversion.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence follows the style rule for fronted negative adverbs?
questions.context: A style reviewer at a San Jose publishing house edits a travel feature about Monteverde.

options.text: Seldom have we seen cloud cover this dense in May.
options.feedback: Correct: seldom is fronted, so the auxiliary have is inverted to the front, before the subject we.

options.text: Seldom we have seen cloud cover this dense in May.
options.feedback: Here the subject we follows the fronted adverbial, so the clause stays in statement order with no inversion.

options.text: We have seldom seen cloud cover this dense in May.
options.feedback: The adverb is in mid-position, so this clause needs no inversion and does not show the fronted pattern.

options.text: Seldom have seen we cloud cover this dense in May.
options.feedback: The verb phrase has been split: only the auxiliary may move in front of the subject, never the object.

questions.explanation:
Fronted seldom or never forces inversion of the auxiliary alone: seldom have we seen it, with the subject right after have.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence is fully correct, with the fronted phrase properly inverted?
questions.context: A fisherman in Parrita waits for the storm to pass before going back to sea.

options.text: Only after the storm passed the fishermen return to the bay.
options.feedback: A fronted only after phrase needs the auxiliary before the subject; here the clause keeps statement order.

options.text: Only after the storm passed did return the fishermen to the bay.
options.feedback: The auxiliary did is fronted, but the subject must follow it directly, before the main verb return.

options.text: Only after the storm passed did the fishermen returned to the bay.
options.feedback: Did carries the tense on its own, so the main verb must be return, not the past participle returned.

options.text: Only after the storm passed did the fishermen return to the bay.
options.feedback: Correct: the fronted phrase triggers inversion, so did precedes the subject and the base verb return closes the clause.

questions.explanation:
Check any inverted clause in this order: fronted phrase, auxiliary, subject, base verb. Breaking one slot makes the sentence wrong.
